comments.author: stochastician
comments.text: The second opinion advice is great, and what I tell everyone I know who gets cancer. My mom was diagnosed with stage 1 cancer in 2006 in Idaho. I was a PhD student at MIT at the time and a friend in lab helped me get an appointment at Dana-Farber. I thought it was probably overkill (it was a common cancer) but we did it anyway. They said everything in Idaho was standard of care but suggested one extra test, which Idaho team then reluctantly did, which revealed distant metastasis (stage 4! ), dramatically changing her treatment trajectory. She lived another 15 years (I miss you Mom). Asking for a second opinion sucks. A lot of us are preconditioned from birth to trust our clinicians. But you're going on a journey and your life (or the life of your loved one) is on the line. Insurance often covers it. Your doctor will NOT be offended. Think of it this way : if you were deploying code to the mars rover, and your colleague asked to do a code review before you pushed go, would you be offended? This is even more important than that.

comments.author: exhilaration
comments.text: My suggestion is that if you're within a 2-3 hour drive of major cancer centers - just use the US News list https://health.usnews.com/best-hospitals/rankings/cancer - go there instead of your local community hospital. The top cancer hospitals in the world accept your health insurance (probably), so why not go there? Use your vacations days, book hotels if you have to - this is the time to go all out. My experience: I was horribly sick for 10 months, none of my local doctors could figure it out, then I drove to Penn Medicine in Philadelphia and they did the right labwork in the first visit. These top centers just have different mindset than your community hospitals.

comments.author: alexpotato
comments.text: Had a family member recently go through unexpected major surgery. One thing I would mention: You are not dealing with a monolithic entity with regards to a hospital. There are really multiple groups with oftentimes competing interests e.g. - case manager wants you out and home b/c that is the best "score" for the hospital. They also DO NOT want you to qualify for Medicare if you are a senior b/c, again, "score" gets dinged if Medicare gets involved - surgeons want you out as they don't want you to pick up hospital infection. They want you to go to a rehab facility as that will more likely lead to a good outcome - the hospitalist wants you to be stable in the short term so will pump you with whatever medications are necessary to get you "back to normal" without addressing any root cause - the nurses generally care about you as a person as they deal with you the most but oftentimes have the least amount of say over your case - in one of those perverse incentives/unintended consequences: if you do TOO well on a physical ability test, that might disqualify you from certain coverage even if you are below the threshold on other ability tests. That can have gigantic insurance implications. This is prompting me to write my own version of the OP blog post.

comments.author: baggachipz
comments.text: The first point is by far the most important. The US healthcare system (and probably others) is an unfeeling machine and you have to treat it that way. Ask for earlier appointments, cancellations, and referrals to other specialists. Navigate it as if nobody knows (or cares) what you're up to. Doctors tend to only exist within their silo and it's often on you to request a different type of doctor or even another one of the same type. Be a pain in the ass, your survival may depend on it. Personal story: I was having trouble using my left arm. Like, couldn't lift or type or do much of anything with it. Was told it was a pinched nerve by physiatrists and orthopedists, despite having no pain. Only when I specifically requested for a referral to a second neurologist did he order the head MRI which exposed a brain tumor in my motor cortex. We were able to move quickly and get me on a treatment plan which has bought me a lot of time. Had I not advocated for myself, it would have probably mutated into a much worse type and killed me soon.

comments.author: runjake
comments.text: This is fantastic. Thanks for posting it, JJ. There's a very strong chance you'll save n>0 lives by posting this. Minor addition: When you talk to someone who has undergone the surgery, try to find someone that's a similar age and in similar shape to you, otherwise you may get wildly varying answers. You'll respond, experience and heal from a surgery quite differently at 40 vs 50.

comments.author: denysvitali
comments.text: Their installer (curl | sh) was taking so long yesterday for me. It turns out it's incredibly slow... because of the progress bar rendering. This is insane. The installer took 6 minutes to reach 10%: curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/v2/install | bash Managed to fix it by running this instead: curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/v2/install | bash 2>&1 | cat

comments.author: solarkraft
comments.text: It's good. Many of the annoyances from V1 are gone. Skills and plugins reload automatically (finally). Tasks can be backgrounded (though I think this doesn't happen automatically yet). There's a built-in skill for editing the configuration (finally I can retire mine). The front-end got some love. Apparently they re-architected the loop around Effect. Sub-sessions can be communicated with better. Configuration is loaded from the folder the session is created in rather than where the server was started. In general, this update largely takes OpenCode into the current age features-wise and is a good overhaul quality-wise. Just in time to stop my early switching away efforts, which would've been a pain because I know few other harnesses with such a strong server/client model.

comments.author: afruitpie
comments.text: Native apps connecting to the OpenCode server is a great way to run sessions on remote hosts! I wish Claude Code would adopt the same model. The desktop app deploys a separate engine that restarts and clobbers long-running sessions upon reconnect (Remote Control is their recommended solution but requires a Claude.ai account). I’ve been vibe coding a native macOS Claude Code app that spawns a server that wraps Claude Code on remote hosts, but the UX and features are always lagging behind.

stories.summary_ja:
## 主な議論点
コミュニティはJev 1.14.0のベンチマークに対する信頼性について懐疑的な意見を示しました。ベンチマークのゲーミング可能性について指摘され、実際のユースケースでのテストの重要性が強調されました。また、マルチモーダル機能が以前のバージョンから既に搭載されていた可能性についての疑問が浮上し、新機能の開示方法について議論が交錯しました。ローカルでの実行可能性やプライバシー重視の需要についても触れられました。

## 賛否両論
**賛成意見**：新しい画像認識機能、特にバウンディングボックスサポートが評価されており、今後のセグメンテーション機能期待の声がありました。ローカルモデルの利便性やCPUでの性能について肯定的なコメントも見られました。

**否定意見**：ベンチマークの信憑性に対する懐疑論が強く、投資者資金による機能開催の疑惑が指摘されました。新機能の過大評価やマーケティング戦略に対する懐疑的な見方が一部から表明されました。

## 注目コメント
「ベンチマークはゲーミング可能な指標。あなたのユースケースで実際にテストする必要がある」というコメントは、コミュニティの懐疑心をよく表しています。また「jev-1.13.0はマルチモーダルだったのではないか」という指摘は、機能開示タイミングに対する考察的なコメントとして注目されました。ローカルモデルの代替案としてOpenDecisionの紹介も興味深い対話を生んでいます。

stories.title_en: Passkeys are not a trap
stories.title_ja: パスキーは罠ではない

comments.author: bonzog
comments.text: I don't know enough to argue about whether passkeys are a trap or not, but I do know as a user that they appear to be a confusing mess. When a website prompts me to set up a passkey, depending on the device I happen to be using at the time it could end up going to Google password manager, Samsung password manager, iCloud Keychain, or Windows somethingorother. What happens when I go to the same site on a different platform? What if I can't use cross-device authentication because I'm on a locked-down work machine or one that simply doesn't have bluetooth? What if I want to consolidate them all in one platform just for the sake of being organised? What if I lose or simply don't have the device with a certain passkey near me? I don't have the time or patience to work out any of that, which might absolutely be a 'me' problem, but TOTPs are pretty sodding frictionless in comparison. Scan QR in my chosen manager; type number into website; done. Why are passkeys better?

comments.author: elgertam
comments.text: I accidentally set up a passkey for one application, a certain accounting software. Now when I login, I'm required to give both the passkey from my password manager and usually my password, too. It's a usability mess and basically makes it impossible for me to share my login with e.g. my wife when she might need to login to that account. That's the practical trap. The real trap is when Google decides in a few years that third party passkey managers will no longer be granted an ability to use the Chrome extension APIs, and Google Sync and other pay-to-play vendors are the only supported ways to handle passkeys. uBlock was just the beginning. I'm sticking with my passwords for now. Some providers ::cough:: Meta ::cough:: have become openly hostile to allowing anyone to login to their services, but most haven't made it too cumbersome yet.

comments.author: coaksford
comments.text: "...if attestation is the thing you're worried about, the post's own recommendation pushes you towards attestation rather than away from it!" It is plainly obvious that the worry isn't attestation per se, it's the restrictions that attestation may in the future require when they turn the dial on restrictiveness up, that was extremely clear to me from reading the first article. If you can get attestation without those restrictions, "sure, why not", and a Yubikey seems like a way to do that which could avoid those restrictions. Most of this article makes sense, but this particular line makes me wonder how the author got it so far off the mark. They also did nothing to quell my fears that they will in the future use passkeys to prevent people from using software they can modify themselves by saying "...the guidance for consumer sites has been to not even request attestation for years now." as if everyone always followed the guidance, and as if there aren't tens of thousands of managers that think their case is special and they really do need the extra control because they're a bank or handle copyrighted content or have PII or PCI and feel extra risk-averse today. I don't know if they failed to do so because they can't (and this is a valid fear of the original author) or if they just are bad at reading the room at what the concern is and vastly overestimate how much people trust companies to always have their best interests at heart. What I am getting from this, though, is "If you authenticate with a yubikey then that's attested, so they can't use attestation through passkeys to make sure your OS and browser aren't modified", and I'm not sure if that's the correct take away or even a correct statement.

comments.author: NoidFonsense
comments.text: This blog post is the perfect example of someone rationalizing away the bigger picture. It's true that passkeys do not require hardware and OS attestation today, so all of the specific examples you cite are true. But the point remains that that passkeys can be EASILY extended to require hardware and OS attestation, and this will happen. Banks have already done this. Before using an app was optional. Play protect was optional. It's like my uncle ted used to say, techonolgy is not optional.

stories.title_en: Do dentists know what they're doing?

comments.author: donatj
comments.text: Like 15 years ago now I had broken a filling. Went in to a new dentist because my insurance had changed. They told me I had 14 cavities, and 3 of my teeth needed crowns - and they were surprisingly rude about the whole ordeal. Reading the reviews on Yelp, someone had said they had a similar experience with their first visit and went to a different dentist and were told they had none. I decided to get a second opinion and heavens am I thankful I did. They replaced my filling right then and there and I think I've had maybe 3 cavities in the 15 years since. I put very little faith in dentists to not be scam artists. The part I find particularly … funny is the disagreements. I had one dentist who insisted I needed to be using a pre-rinse. That dentist ended up leaving, and a different dentist at THE SAME OFFICE told me it was a waste of money and I should stop because it does nothing. I swear they all just make it up as they go. I've had multiple dentists tell me this rough tooth in the back of my mouth needed to be capped because it was "falling apart". I started using imported NovaMin on it out of curiosity and it became super smooth instead of rough and no one has mentioned it since. One dentist I saw for a number of years would try to insist I needed a dental implant for a missing molar and if I didn't all my teeth were going to come out alignment. I didn't have money for it at the time. Not a single dentist before or since has mentioned this.

comments.author: tkdb
comments.text: I'm surprised that there isn't more attention being paid to this question: How does dental (or medical) care differ when the person recommending the procedure directly benefits financially from it? I've had experiences with doctors who make exactly the same if they perform a $1,000 procedure or a $10,000 procedure, and I feel in general I'm likely to get better care in that scenario. (In the US) I regularly scrutinize and stress over the dentist's recommendations, as they are almost always the owner of the business as well as the head dental procedure recommender.

comments.author: NichoPaolucci
comments.text: Dentists, orthodontists, periodontists... I feel the same. I'm a real case study, I was born without my 4 permanent lateral incisors (Top and bottom). First orthodontist applied braces too early in my life - also decided that "eventually" implants would be placed on the bottom, moved my two bottom front teeth to the sides to create one large gap. (This was disapproved of by my second orthodontist). Once an adult, my dentist recommended a new ortho + perio. The periodontist recommended an experimental procedure called "Periodontally Assisted Osteogenic Orthodontics". Which involved... filleting my gums to the bone, while I was awake. Later, the dentist said he totally should have sedated me for that procedure. It was one of the most brutal experiences of my life, not joking, like... Actual torture. The perio then placed two implants on the top. My dentist later disapproved of this, saying they were 'far too small'. One of the implants failed within 3 years. The other is barely hanging on. And the bottom could not have an implant placed, because the PAOO did not work (Surprise, I still owed 7200 dollars). I've been in and out of these offices so much that I started picking up their jargon - two have asked if I'm IN dental school when we discuss treatment. All that to say, these people seem to be winging it. I get it, every mouth is different, but man... It's such an important fixture socially / health-wise that I feel we should be doing better. If anyone knows a good cosmetic dentist, I'm still in the search for one :)

comments.author: joshstrange
comments.text: > Poor form. A good dentist should have more professional curiosity than this. I find _very little_ "professional curiosity" exists overall. Heck, I don't even always see it within our industry where I think it's maybe more common? Maybe I'm biased. s/dentists/doctors I'm reading up on new tech stuff all the time and it shocks me that most of the doctors I've ever interacted with don't seem to be doing the same. It's like they are just coasting on what they learned in school. And since the vast majority of us only see 1 doctor of a given type at best once a year (maybe more for the dentist, but the same dentist) we never get any sort of "second opinion". Think about all the people you've worked with in tech, now think about them being the sole-decider for how to architect/build something without any pushback or anyone else to push back or give advice. Yeah, that's how I imagine the whole medical field. Implement drainAndCloseBodyWithTimer // Team: no problems here 3. then drainAsyncAndCloseBodyWithTimer // Team: a bit wordy but no problem here 4. Someone at google uses 3. with an http/2 connection // Team: this is where we draw the line? However, I'm also missing, if I want to slam this connection closed, which is a reasonable thing to want, how do I do that without uselessly draining a socket I don't intend to reuse? Fake the "Connection: close" header into the Response object? Hope I can dig out an underlying socket of some sort under the concrete type of the Body.Response that I can bypass this code with? stories.summary_ja:
Go 1.27 の net/http がレスポンスボディを自動的にドレインしてコネクションを再利用可能にする仕組みが主な話題となった。具体的には drainAndCloseBody 系の関数が導入され、HTTP/2 コネクションでも自動的にドレインされるようになった点が議論の中心で、ドキュメント不足や json.Decoder が改行を残すと再利用が妨げられるケースも挙げられた。また、HTTP/3 を標準ライブラリに組み込んでほしいという要望も見られた。  

賛否両論については、自動ドレインによりコードが簡潔になり、サードパーティ製ラッパーが不要になる利点を評価する声がある一方、意図せずボディを読み込むのは無駄であり、接続をすぐに閉じたいときに適切な API が見当たらないという不満も多い。特に「Connection: close」ヘッダーを偽装したり内部ソケットに直接アクセスする裏技を探すコメントが注目され、ドレインせずに終了する方法の提供を求める意見が目立った。  

注目コメントとして、あるユーザーは「ドレインせずにソケットを閉じる手段が欲しい」と明言し、標準 API に明示的な Close オプションが必要だと指摘；もう一つは json.Decoder の More メソッドで残りの空白をドレインすればコネクション再利用を復帰できると助言している点が実践的な洞察として挙げられた。
stories.editor_note: Go 1.27 での HTTP/1 コネクション再利用の改善

comments.text: This has actually been a trend since the 1960s: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowling_Alone The simple answer is media. First television, then internet, then smartphones. People used to actively seek the company of others - if for no other reason than out of boredom. Entertainment and parasocial relationships have filled that hole. Another reason I might posit is declining birth rates and an aging population. Entire neighborhoods used to be filled with young families of roughly the same age. Now on any given city block in the US, there may only be 1 or 2 houses that have kids of any age in them. Smaller concentration of kids -> thinner market for playdates and sleepovers -> less interactions between families.

comments.text: I am 36 and I have been thinking about suicide a tiny bit lately. But I will share my perspective with you, hopefully to draw a picture how different circumstances can be. I live in Ukraine and my optionality in life collapsed the day the war started. I had a good life, good income and traveled a lot. I used to dream of a career in big tech and life in different countries just to give it a taste. Now I am not able to leave the country because I am a male of conscription age. My city is being attacked by drones daily, and ballistic rockets a few times a month. Witnessing your country getting wrecked with rockets and drones is hell of an experience. Businesses, electricity plants, infrastructure, gas stations becoming rubble. There is also little hope in a resolution of this soon. I have to work on a job which provides a reservation from military service if I don’t want to fight, otherwise I will be picked up on the street to join the military. I have it so much better than a lot of my countrymen, but holy shit does this suck and it is not getting better anytime soon. The hopelessness gets you. Software engineering is one of my last remaining pillars of life remaining more or less intact. At least I get to write some code and make computers do things. Life is a strange thing.

comments.author: munificent
comments.text: Because it's highly relevant, I'm going to paraphrase a comment I made last week: I think a big part of the problem is that middle-aged men are at the apex of their expectations to be successful in the eyes of society, and we are living through a period of time where success is very hard to define, much less attain. There is a name for this in sociology: anomie [1]. Émile Durkheim coined it in his book Suicide , written not too long after the Industrial Revolution. In times of great change, the set of norms and rules that we take for granted as an organizing principle of our lives get uprooted. It's as if all of the pieces and tokens and rules of the board game we played our whole lives are swept off the table to make room for a new game, but the new game has not been set up yet. In that interim, we all feel a sense of unease. It is our turn to move, but we don't know the rules of the game or what moves to make. We feel intense pressure to play the game well, but don't know how. In the past, these transitions have ended and society has generally returned to some sense of stability. A new board game gets set up, new pieces doled out, we learn to play the new game. I hope we get to that point with AI soon, but the revolutions seem to keep coming faster and faster. I think for a lot of men, it feels like just at the time when we should be able to rest on our laurels a bit after having worked so hard to play the game society told us to, the rules have been ripped out from under us and any sense of security going forward is lost. comments.author: devy
comments.text: A couple preliminary findings if you are considering adopting this extension to replace your previous pgvector's HNSW indexing. - pg_vectorsearch uses a quantized IVF index called PRISM. PRISM caps at 1968 dimensions for vectors. If your previous HNSW index has more dimensions than that, you're SOL (at least for now until they fix that). - pg_vectorsearch requires Postgres version 18 or above. If you run PG versions below that you need to migrate your database first. Many legacy PG production environment are way dated on PG 14 or 15, migration is prohibitively high cost to just try this out. - pg_vectorsearch shipped yesterday and it's obviously alpha. Hasn't been battle tested in production environments outside of Timescale's. Also since it's so new, it isn't on Azure's allowed-extension list or any other Hyperscale's managed PG instances' allowed extension list. It takes time to graduate from alpha and mature. So if you run managaed PG instances from hyperscaler's cloud, you're SOL (at least for now until this matures into those ecosystems) or you have to migrate to a PG 18 self-hosted.

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、希土類産業のボトルネックが採掘ではなく分離・精錬にあること、2015年の中国による市場供給過多で米国企業が撤退しマウンテンパス鉱山が停止した歴史、そしてエネルギー・労働・環境規制・法的コストと規模経済が価格シグナルとして海外移転を促した点である。さらに、「失った」か「売り渡した」かという言葉の定義や、稀土類に常に伴うトリウムの核利用可能性、そして現在のスタートアップが主張する新しい分離技術の実現可能性が論じられた。賛否両論として、一部は分離技術スタートアップが解決策になると期待するが、多くは資金調達規模が小さく、実証プランツの遅れや過去の失敗例から懐疑的である。また、価格シグナルへの肯定的見解と、グローバル化への依存を危惧する意見が対立した。注目コメントでは、稀土類は実は豊富だがトリウムと共存し分離が困難であることを指摘し、さらに「閉山は損失であり、単なる売却ではない」という観点から、アイドル状態の鉄鋼プラント例を挙げて用語の semantics を問う洞察があった。
